title: Chess: Openings, Tactics, Terms

sources.name: Original educational synthesis from general knowledge
FIDE Laws of Chess: rule reference

description: For beginning chess players learning opening names, tactical patterns, notation and core strategic terms. Original examples use standard chess positions and algebraic move notation.

cards.front: What is a file in chess?
cards.back: A vertical column of squares, labeled a through h.
cards.example: The e-file contains e1 through e8.

cards.front: What is a rank in chess?
cards.back: A horizontal row of squares, labeled 1 through 8.
cards.example: White's initial back rank is rank 1.

cards.front: What is a diagonal in chess?
cards.back: A line of squares touching corner to corner, all of the same color.
cards.example: The a1–h8 diagonal has eight squares.

cards.front: Which four squares form the central four-square area?
cards.back: d4, e4, d5, and e5.
cards.example: Central pawns often contest these squares.

cards.back: Along a rank or file any unobstructed distance.
cards.example: A rook can move from a1 to a4 if a2 and a3 are clear.

cards.back: Diagonally any unobstructed distance.
cards.example: A bishop stays on one square color throughout the game.

cards.back: Along ranks, files, or diagonals any unobstructed distance.
cards.example: A queen combines rook-like and bishop-like movement.

cards.back: Two squares in one direction and one perpendicular, jumping over intervening pieces.
cards.example: A knight on e4 can move to f6.

cards.front: How does a king ordinarily move?
cards.back: One square in any direction, without moving into check.
cards.example: A king can move from e1 to f1 if the square is legal.

cards.front: How does a pawn ordinarily advance?
cards.back: One square forward into an empty square; from its starting square it may move two if both squares are clear.
cards.example: White can begin with e2–e4.

cards.front: How does a pawn ordinarily capture?
cards.back: One square diagonally forward.
cards.example: A white pawn on e4 can capture an enemy piece on d5.

cards.back: A pawn reaching the farthest rank must become a queen, rook, bishop, or knight of its color.
cards.example: A pawn reaching a8 can promote to a queen.

cards.back: Promoting a pawn to a rook, bishop, or knight rather than a queen.
cards.example: A knight promotion can give a useful fork.

cards.back: An immediate pawn capture of an adjacent enemy pawn that just advanced two squares, as if it had advanced one.
cards.example: A white pawn on e5 may capture d6 after Black plays d7–d5.

cards.front: What is castling in standard chess?
cards.back: A special king-and-rook move: the king moves two squares toward the rook and the rook crosses to the adjacent square.
cards.example: White kingside castling places the king on g1 and rook on f1.

cards.front: What movement history forbids castling with a particular rook?
cards.back: Any prior move by the king or that rook, even if it returned.
cards.example: Moving the king and returning it to e1 loses both castling rights.

cards.front: Can a king castle out of, through, or into check?
cards.back: No.
cards.example: White cannot castle kingside if f1 is attacked.

cards.front: Must the squares between king and rook be empty for standard castling?
cards.back: Yes.
cards.example: White queenside castling requires b1, c1, and d1 to be empty.

cards.front: Does an attacked rook alone prevent castling?
cards.back: No, provided all castling conditions for the king and clear path are satisfied.
cards.example: An attacked h1 rook does not by itself forbid kingside castling.

cards.back: An attack on the opponent's king that requires a legal response.
cards.example: A rook attacking the king along an open file gives check.

cards.front: What are the general ways to answer a single check?
cards.back: Move the king, capture the checking piece, or block the line when possible.
cards.example: A knight check cannot be blocked by interposition.

cards.back: The king is in check and the player has no legal move that removes the check.
cards.example: The game ends immediately when a legal move delivers mate.

cards.back: The player to move is not in check but has no legal move; the game is drawn.
cards.example: A trapped lone king can be stalemated if no square is legal.

cards.front: Can a king legally move next to the opposing king?
cards.back: No. Kings attack adjacent squares.
cards.example: The kings must not occupy adjacent squares.

cards.front: What does N stand for in English algebraic notation?
cards.back: Knight.
cards.example: Nf3 denotes a knight move to f3 when unambiguous.

cards.front: What does x indicate in algebraic move notation?
cards.back: A capture.
cards.example: Bxe5 means a bishop captures on e5.

cards.front: What does + indicate after a move?
cards.back: Check.
cards.example: Qh5+ means the move gives check.

cards.front: What does # indicate after a move?
cards.back: Checkmate.
cards.example: Qh7# denotes mate.

cards.back: Kingside castling.
cards.example: White's king finishes on g1.

cards.back: Queenside castling.
cards.example: White's king finishes on c1.

cards.back: Bringing pieces into active positions, especially in the opening.
cards.example: Moving a knight from g1 to f3 develops it.

cards.back: A single move considered as a unit of useful time.
cards.example: Developing with a threat can gain a tempo.

cards.back: An opening offer of material, usually a pawn, for compensation.
cards.example: A player may sacrifice a pawn for rapid development.

cards.back: Reaching the same position by a different move order.
cards.example: Two opening sequences can lead to identical positions.

cards.back: A player's prepared set of opening choices and plans.
cards.example: A repertoire may include one response to 1.e4 and another to 1.d4.

cards.front: Why is early king safety an opening priority?
cards.back: An exposed king can become a tactical target before defenses coordinate.
cards.example: Timely castling often connects safety with development.

cards.front: Why can repeated early moves with one piece waste time?
cards.back: Other pieces remain undeveloped while the opponent improves coordination.
cards.example: A queen repeatedly chased by minor pieces can lose tempi.

cards.back: The Ruy Lopez, also called the Spanish Opening.
cards.example: White pressures the knight defending e5.

cards.back: The Italian Game.
cards.example: The bishop points toward f7.

cards.back: The Scotch Game.
cards.example: White immediately challenges the center with d4.

cards.back: The King's Gambit.
cards.example: White offers the f-pawn to challenge e5.

cards.back: The Sicilian Defense.
cards.example: Black contests d4 with the c-pawn.

cards.front: What defense begins 1.e4 e6, commonly followed by 2.d4 d5?
cards.back: The French Defense.
cards.example: Black prepares a central challenge with d5.

cards.front: What defense begins 1.e4 c6, commonly followed by 2.d4 d5?
cards.back: The Caro-Kann Defense.
cards.example: The c-pawn supports d5.

cards.back: The Scandinavian Defense.
cards.example: Black immediately attacks the e4 pawn.

cards.back: Alekhine's Defense.
cards.example: Black invites White's central pawns to advance.

cards.front: What opening family commonly begins 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6?
cards.back: The Pirc Defense.
cards.example: Black develops a kingside fianchetto against a broad center.

cards.back: The Modern Defense.
cards.example: Black often develops the bishop to g7 before committing the king's knight.

cards.back: The Queen's Gambit.
cards.example: White challenges Black's d5 pawn with the c-pawn.

cards.back: The Queen's Gambit Declined.
cards.example: Black supports d5 rather than capturing c4 immediately.

cards.back: The Queen's Gambit Accepted.
cards.example: Black captures the offered c-pawn.

cards.back: The Slav Defense.
cards.example: Black supports d5 with the c-pawn.

cards.front: What defense begins 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4?
cards.back: The Nimzo-Indian Defense.
cards.example: The bishop pins the c3 knight to the king.

cards.front: What defense commonly begins 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6?
cards.back: The King's Indian Defense.
cards.example: Black allows a large white center before counterattacking.

cards.front: What defense begins 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5?
cards.back: The Grünfeld Defense.
cards.example: Black strikes at White's center with d5.

cards.back: The Dutch Defense.
cards.example: Black uses the f-pawn to contest e4.

cards.front: What is the usual first move of the English Opening?
cards.example: White controls d5 from the flank.

cards.front: What move commonly starts the Réti opening family?
cards.back: 1.Nf3, often followed by c4 against a d5 setup.
cards.example: White delays occupying the center with a central pawn.

cards.front: What is a typical London System setup for White?
cards.back: A d4 center with an early Bf4, commonly supported by Nf3 and e3.
cards.example: The dark-squared bishop develops before e3 blocks it.

cards.back: Developing a bishop to b2, g2, b7, or g7 behind an advanced adjacent pawn.
cards.example: White plays g3 and Bg2.

cards.front: What is an open game in opening classification?
cards.back: A game beginning 1.e4 e5.
cards.example: The Italian Game is an open-game opening.

cards.front: What is a semi-open game in opening classification?
cards.back: A game beginning 1.e4 with a Black response other than 1...e5.
cards.example: The Sicilian is semi-open in this classification.

cards.back: A short, concrete sequence exploiting threats or vulnerabilities.
cards.example: A forcing sequence wins an undefended piece.

cards.back: One piece simultaneously attacks multiple enemy targets.
cards.example: A knight attacks a king and queen at once.

cards.back: A move creating two simultaneous threats, whether made by one piece or through coordinated attacks by different pieces.
cards.example: A move uncovers one attack while making another.

cards.back: An attacked piece cannot or should not move because a more important target lies behind it.
cards.example: A bishop attacks a knight shielding a queen.

cards.back: A pin to the king, making moves that expose the king illegal.
cards.example: A knight between an enemy rook and its king is absolutely pinned along that line.
cards.hint: Consider which piece is behind the pinned unit.

cards.back: A pin to a valuable target other than the king; moving is legal but may lose material.
cards.example: A bishop pins a knight to a queen.

cards.back: A line attack on a valuable front piece that may expose a piece behind when it moves.
cards.example: A rook checks the king while attacking a rook behind it.

cards.back: Moving one piece uncovers an attack by another.
cards.example: A knight moves away to open a bishop's line to the queen.

cards.back: A discovered attack specifically against the king.
cards.example: Moving a bishop uncovers a rook check.

cards.back: Two pieces give check simultaneously, normally after a discovered-check move.
cards.example: The checked side must respond with a king move.

cards.back: Forcing or enticing a defender away from an important duty.
cards.example: A sacrifice draws a rook away from guarding mate.

cards.back: Drawing an enemy piece to a particular vulnerable square.
cards.example: A sacrifice lures the king into a fork.

cards.front: What is removal of the defender?
cards.back: Capturing or otherwise eliminating a piece that protects a target.
cards.example: Trading off a defender leaves a rook loose.

cards.back: A defender has more duties than it can successfully fulfill.
cards.example: A rook cannot both guard mate and protect a queen after a forcing move.

cards.back: Blocking an enemy line of defense or communication.
cards.example: A piece interposes between a bishop and a defended square.

cards.back: Vacating a square or line so another piece can use it.
cards.example: A knight moves away to open a rook's file.

cards.back: An intermediate move inserted before an expected response.
cards.example: A player gives check before recapturing.

cards.back: Deliberately giving material for tactical or positional compensation.
cards.example: A bishop is offered to expose the enemy king.

cards.back: Giving a rook for a minor piece, usually a bishop or knight.
cards.example: A rook captures a knight and is recaptured by a pawn.

cards.back: A piece vulnerable to capture without adequate compensation, often because it is undefended.
cards.example: An unprotected bishop can be taken for free.

cards.back: A piece with little or no protection, potentially vulnerable to tactics.
cards.example: A knight fork can exploit two loose pieces.

cards.back: Coordinated control of escape squares and checking routes that threatens or forces mate.
cards.example: Pieces progressively restrict the king's safe squares.

cards.back: Mate against a king on its home rank with escape blocked, often by its own pawns.
cards.example: A rook checks along the eighth rank while pawns block the king.

cards.back: A knight delivers mate to a king trapped by its own pieces.
cards.example: The knight checks a king with no available neighboring square.

cards.back: A sequence allowing repeated checks that the defender cannot escape without disadvantage; a draw can follow by repetition or agreement.
cards.example: The attacker keeps checking instead of allowing a losing endgame.

cards.back: A file containing no pawns of either color.
cards.example: Rooks often use open files to enter the opponent's position.

cards.back: A file with no pawn of one's own color but at least one enemy pawn.
cards.example: A rook can pressure the enemy pawn along that file.

cards.back: A useful advanced square for a piece that is difficult for enemy pawns to challenge, often pawn-supported.
cards.example: A knight settles on a protected central square.

cards.back: A pawn with no friendly pawn on either adjacent file.
cards.example: An isolated d-pawn lacks friendly c- and e-pawns.

cards.back: Two friendly pawns on the same file.
cards.example: A capture can leave pawns on c2 and c3.

cards.back: A pawn with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or adjacent files.
cards.example: It has no opposing pawn able to stop it by advancing or capturing from those files.

cards.back: A pawn lagging behind neighboring friendly pawns that cannot advance safely.
cards.example: An enemy piece controls its advance square.

cards.back: A diagonal formation of mutually linked pawns, where rear pawns defend those ahead.
cards.example: White pawns on c3, d4, and e5 form a chain.

cards.back: A pawn move challenging the opponent's pawn structure, often opening lines.
cards.example: Black plays c5 against a white d4 center.

cards.front: What is space in chess strategy?
cards.back: The area available for effective piece movement and maneuvering.
cards.example: Advanced central pawns can give one side more space.

cards.back: The ability to create threats that require the opponent's attention.
cards.example: Active pieces keep forcing defensive replies.

cards.back: Preventing or reducing an opponent's plan or threat.
cards.example: A quiet king move avoids a future checking tactic.

cards.back: A position in which having to move worsens one's situation.
cards.example: A king must give up a key square in a pawn ending.

cards.front: What is opposition in a king endgame?
cards.back: A relationship where kings face each other with an odd number of intervening squares, often one, and the side not to move can force the other to yield.
cards.example: Kings on e4 and e6 have direct opposition.

cards.back: A maneuver that loses a move to reach a similar position with the opponent to move.
cards.example: A king takes a three-move route instead of a two-move route.

cards.front: What is the rule of the square for a passed pawn?
cards.back: A geometric shortcut for judging whether a king can catch an unobstructed advancing pawn, accounting for whose turn it is and any initial double move.
cards.example: Draw a square from the pawn toward its promotion rank.

cards.back: A defensive setup that prevents progress despite a material disadvantage.
cards.example: The stronger side cannot create a legal breakthrough.

cards.back: Possession of both a light-squared and a dark-squared bishop.
cards.example: Together they can influence both square colors.

cards.back: A bishop restricted by its own pawns on the same color squares.
cards.example: A closed pawn chain blocks the bishop's routes.

cards.front: What is an active king in the endgame?
cards.back: A king used to attack, defend, and control key squares once mating danger is manageable.
cards.example: The king approaches enemy pawns.

cards.front: What is a dead position under the basic chess rules?
cards.back: A position in which neither side can checkmate by any possible series of legal moves; it is drawn.
cards.example: King against king is a dead position.

cards.front: What is a threefold-repetition draw under FIDE rules?
cards.back: A draw claim based on the same position occurring at least three times with the same player to move and the same legal possibilities, using the proper procedure.
cards.example: Lost castling rights can make similar-looking positions different.

cards.front: What is the fifty-move draw rule under FIDE rules?
cards.back: A player may claim a draw after fifty moves by each player without a pawn move or capture, including the prescribed intended-move procedure.
cards.example: A pawn move resets the count.

cards.back: A comparison of the pieces and pawns each side has.
cards.example: A rook versus a bishop is often called an exchange advantage.
